decisive_items: He had traveled to Sudan 6 months previously
striking infiltration of the eyelids and periorbital skin with multiple firm tumorous swellings of the forehead and temples
The hands and fingers were swollen with scattered focal purpuric infarcts
response.rationale: Sudanese exposure, diffuse facial/periorbital infiltration with tumorous swellings, rippled skin, and purpuric infarcts are characteristic of lepromatous leprosy, particularly with Lucio phenomenon. The histiocytic and granulomatous inflammation with neutrophilic abscesses fits a leprosy reaction, while other candidates lack this combination of endemic exposure, leonine infiltration, and vascular purpuric lesions.

rejected.why: Erythema nodosum leprosum is a leprosy reaction, but the rippled infiltration and purpuric infarcts better fit diffuse lepromatous leprosy/Lucio phenomenon rather than classic ENL.
Necrobiotic xanthogranuloma can involve periorbital skin but lacks endemic exposure, purpuric infarcts, and neutrophilic abscesses; typically associated with paraproteinemia and xanthomatous plaques.
Relapsing polychondritis does not explain the facial tumorous infiltration, rippled skin, purpuric infarcts, or deep dermal mucin.
Granuloma annulare can show mucin and histiocytes, but it does not cause facial tumorous swellings, purpuric infarcts, or systemic drowsiness and weakness.
Granulomatosis with polyangiitis can have granulomatous inflammation and purpuric lesions, but normal chest imaging, absence of renal/upper airway involvement, and deep dermal mucin make it unlikely.
Erythema nodosum explains subcutaneous neutrophilic panniculitis and elevated CRP, but not the facial infiltration, rippled skin, purpuric infarcts, or Sudan exposure.
Leishmaniasis is plausible due to Sudan travel and histiocytic infiltrate, but it does not explain rippled skin, purpuric infarcts, or deep dermal mucin, and no amastigotes were identified.
Cutaneous leishmaniasis shares facial swelling and travel history, but lacks the characteristic rippled skin, purpuric infarcts, and deep dermal mucin; no parasitological confirmation is provided.
